findings.requirement_type: Convex Excess — Schedule of Underlying Policy Number Discrepancy
findings.contract_quote: N/A — administrative defect.
findings.policy_quote: Dec page Item 5 shows Gemini policy VIPL056495; Schedule of Underlying Insurance (XPL-301, page 13) shows VIPL055885. Both Gemini, but the policy number doesn't match.
findings.gap_description: Convex Dec page references Gemini policy number VIPL056495; Schedule of Underlying lists VIPL055885. Both are Gemini Tech E&O policies but the numbers don't match. In a coverage dispute, a defense attorney could argue the excess policy doesn't actually sit over the bound Gemini policy. Administrative defect, but worth correcting before claim time.
findings.plain_english: Your Convex excess policy lists two different Gemini policy numbers in two different places. Almost certainly a clerical error, but in a coverage dispute the carrier could argue the excess doesn't actually sit over the Gemini policy you have. Five-minute fix at the broker — get an endorsement aligning the numbers.
findings.recommendation: Request Convex issue an endorsement correcting the Schedule of Underlying to match the Dec page Gemini policy number. Confirm with Gemini which policy number is current.
discoveryQuestions: Your excess policy lists Gemini policy VIPL056495 on the dec but VIPL055885 on the schedule of underlying. In a coverage dispute, defense attorneys win on details like this — has the broker requested a correcting endorsement?

findings.requirement_type: Hartford Crime — Virtual Currency $15K Sublimit
findings.contract_quote: N/A — internal coverage limitation.
findings.policy_quote: Crime Coverage Part: Virtual Currency Sublimit Per Occurrence $15,000 / Retention $5,000 per Occurrence.
findings.gap_description: Crime Virtual Currency sublimit at $15K is low. Less critical for an election services vendor that likely has minimal crypto exposure, but if any vendor invoices, ransomware payments, or experimental payment rails involve crypto, capacity is inadequate. Note that AmTrust Cyber excludes virtual currency from Crime IA #2 carve-back.
findings.plain_english: Crypto-related theft is capped at $15K under Crime. Probably fine for now — election services isn't a crypto-heavy industry — but worth flagging if your operations evolve.
findings.recommendation: Maintain current limit. Re-evaluate if crypto exposure grows.
discoveryQuestions: Do any of your vendor relationships, contractor payments, or operational activities involve cryptocurrency? If yes, your Crime coverage caps at $15K — if no, this is a non-issue.

Has anyone proposed crypto rails for any segment of your operations? Many election technology firms are evaluating blockchain-based audit trails — if you're heading there, this sublimit needs re-sizing.

findings.requirement_type: Hartford D&O — Antitrust / Unfair Trade Practices Sublimited to $1M
findings.contract_quote: N/A — internal coverage limitation.
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #16 (PP 00 H377 00 0120 — Anti Trust/Unfair Trade Exclusion Sublimit): 'Antitrust/Sherman/Clayton/FTC violations subject to sublimit of lesser of remaining limit or $1,000,000. Carve-back from total exclusion to sublimited coverage.'
findings.gap_description: Antitrust / unfair trade practices claims sublimited to $1M (or remaining limit if less). Better than full exclusion but still capped. Election services is a concentrated industry with limited number of players (Runbeck, ES&S, Dominion, Hart, etc.) — antitrust exposure (price-fixing allegations, market allocation, exclusive county contract disputes) is a foreseeable scenario in litigious election cycles. $1M of defense costs evaporates quickly in a federal antitrust matter.
findings.plain_english: Antitrust claims are capped at $1M under your D&O. The election technology industry has only a few major players, and antitrust litigation among them or alleging anticompetitive conduct is a foreseeable scenario. $1M doesn't cover much federal antitrust defense — these matters routinely run $5M-$20M in defense alone. Worth pushing the sublimit higher at renewal.
findings.recommendation: At renewal: negotiate antitrust sublimit removal or increase to $5M+. Industry-specific framing (election services concentrated market, limited competitors, county-by-county contract dynamics) supports underwriter willingness to expand.
discoveryQuestions: The election technology market has only a handful of major players. If a competitor or county alleged price-fixing, market allocation, or exclusive-dealing, your D&O covers $1M of antitrust defense. Federal antitrust matters routinely cost $5M-$20M to defend. Comfortable with that gap?
Has Run-Test ever been involved in a competitive dispute with another election services vendor? Bid protests on county contracts? Aggressive market positioning? Each is a potential antitrust trigger.
PE sponsors generally want robust D&O on the antitrust line because PE deals concentrate market share. Have Lincoln Shields and Black Mountain reviewed this $1M sublimit?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa COI Renewal Cadence (15-Day) and Sacramento (10-Day)
findings.contract_quote: (Maricopa §8.2.14) If a policy does expire during the life of the Contract, a renewal certificate must be sent to County 15 calendar days prior to the expiration date. (Sacramento §VI.A.2) The Contractor shall maintain all insurance coverages and limits in place at all times and provide the County with evidence of each policy's renewal ten (10) days in advance of its anniversary date.
findings.contract_page: Maricopa §8.2.14, Page 7 of 41; Sacramento §VI.A.2, Page 3 of 4
findings.policy_quote: N/A — administrative obligation, not policy language.
findings.gap_description: Both contracts impose pre-renewal certificate delivery obligations: Maricopa 15 calendar days prior to expiration, Sacramento 10 calendar days prior to anniversary. Not a policy gap — an administrative compliance requirement that requires documented agency calendar management. Most agency renewal cycles fail to consistently meet these windows. Failure to meet is a contract breach.
findings.plain_english: Both counties require renewal COIs in advance — Maricopa wants 15 days, Sacramento wants 10 days before policy anniversary. This is an administrative obligation, not an insurance gap. Build it into the agency calendar. Missing the window is technically a contract breach even if coverage is bound timely.
findings.recommendation: Build a renewal-cycle calendar at the broker level: 30 days before each policy expiration, generate renewal COIs and deliver to both Sacramento and Maricopa Risk Management with delivery confirmation. Track in agency management system.
discoveryQuestions: Maricopa requires renewal COIs 15 days before expiration; Sacramento wants 10 days. Does your agency have a tickler system that delivers COIs that early? Most agencies deliver same-day or 1-2 days before — that's a contract breach.
If a renewal COI is delivered late and the County terminates for material breach, what's your contract-revenue exposure? Probably worth solving the 15-day delivery cadence.

findings.requirement_type: Endorsement Copies Required with COI (Sacramento)
findings.contract_quote: Copies of required endorsements must be attached to provided certificates. ... All certificates, evidences of self-insurance, and additional insured endorsements are to be received and approved by the County before performance commences. The COUNTY reserves the right to require that CONTRACTOR provide complete, certified copies of any policy of insurance offered in compliance with these specifications.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — administrative obligation.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §I requires endorsement copies to accompany the COI — not just COI itself. Many agencies overlook this requirement and deliver bare COIs. Sacramento may also demand certified policy copies. Pre-performance County approval also required, which means contracts can't begin until County signs off on insurance compliance.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento doesn't just want a COI — they want copies of the actual endorsements (AI, P&NC, WoS, completed-ops AI) attached. And they reserve the right to demand the entire policy. Build this into your COI delivery workflow or you'll be flagged at the next contract review.
findings.recommendation: Standard COI package for Sacramento submissions should include: (1) ACORD COI; (2) AI endorsement copies (CG 20 10 / CG 20 37 — once Finding 005 is fixed); (3) P&NC endorsement copy (CG 20 01); (4) WoS endorsement copy (CG 24 04); (5) WC AI/WoS endorsement copies (WC 00 03 13, WC 04 03 06). Pre-stage these with carrier requests at renewal.
discoveryQuestions: Sacramento's contract requires endorsement copies attached to your COI. Has your agency been delivering full endorsement packages, or just bare COIs? Most agencies miss this.
Has Sacramento ever requested certified copies of your full policies? They have the contractual right — and increasingly, county Risk Managers exercise it on cyber and E&O specifically.

findings.requirement_type: Inland Marine Policy Absent — High-Value Election Equipment Exposure
findings.contract_quote: Inland Marine Waiver of Subrogation: Any Inland Marine insurance policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall be endorsed to state that the insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: No Inland Marine policy located in program. Hanover Property covers BPP (Blanket Personal Property $16,280,820) for property at scheduled premises. BPP Off-Premises sublimit $250,000; In Transit $100,000. Property in transit on CGL Coverage Extension $5,000.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §IX contemplates Inland Marine policies and requires WoS if any are in place. Run-Test's client notes flag 'High-value equipment' as a special risk. Election technology equipment (ballot tabulators, scanners, mail sorters, ballot processing machines) deployed at county sites is exactly the inland marine exposure profile. The Hanover Property BPP only provides $250K Off-Premises and $100K In Transit — wholly inadequate for high-value election equipment that may individually exceed $250K per unit. There is no monoline Inland Marine, no Equipment Floater, and no Bailee's Customer Goods coverage in the program. Property at county sites is NOT adequately covered for fire/theft/transit damage.
findings.plain_english: You deploy expensive election equipment at county sites — tabulators, scanners, mail sorters, ballot processing machines. Your property policy only covers $250K of that off-premises. A single piece of high-value election technology can exceed that. There's no Inland Marine policy in your program. If a $500K tabulator is destroyed at a county site, you collect $250K. The 'High-value equipment' exposure flagged in your client profile is genuinely uninsured at scale.
findings.recommendation: (1) Inventory all election technology equipment by location and value (deployed at county sites + in transit + at Run-Test premises). (2) Quote Equipment Floater / Inland Marine policy with limits matching peak deployment exposure ($1M-$5M depending on inventory). (3) Endorse Sacramento and Maricopa as loss payees / additional insureds where appropriate per contract. (4) Add Bailee's Customer Goods coverage if Run-Test holds county-owned equipment for repair/storage.
findings.covered_by_which_policy: Hanover Property BPP responds at $250K Off-Premises / $100K In Transit only — material under-insurance for high-value election equipment.
discoveryQuestions: What's the deployed value of your election technology equipment at county sites at peak election cycle? Tabulators, scanners, sorters — single units can run $50K-$500K+. Your property policy covers $250K total off-premises. Is the gap modeled?

Have you ever had equipment damaged in transit to a county or while deployed on-site? How was the loss covered? If it was a small loss, the Property policy probably worked — but a single major loss exceeds the off-premises sublimit easily.
Do you ever hold county-owned equipment for repair, storage, or upgrade? That's bailee exposure — and it's not covered anywhere in your current program.

What does your competitive set carry for Inland Marine? Most election technology vendors carry $1M-$5M of equipment floater coverage with carrier-specific endorsements naming county loss payees. You're materially under-insured on this line.

findings.requirement_type: AmTrust Cyber — Choice of Law (New York) for AZ-Domiciled Insured
findings.contract_quote: N/A — material policy mechanic deserving disclosure.
findings.policy_quote: Choice of Law: New York.
findings.gap_description: Cyber policy applies New York choice-of-law in coverage disputes. Insured is AZ-domiciled with operations in 31+ states. NY law differs from AZ law on bad-faith damages, recoverable categories, statute of limitations, attorneys' fees recovery, and punitive damage availability. Material in any future coverage litigation. Worth a coverage attorney review at next renewal.
findings.plain_english: Your cyber policy uses New York law in coverage disputes. You're an Arizona company. NY and AZ law differ meaningfully on bad-faith damages and other policyholder protections. It's a contractual choice you made (probably without realizing it) — worth understanding the implications.
findings.recommendation: Request coverage attorney review of NY-vs-AZ-law implications at next renewal. If AZ law is materially more policyholder-friendly, request choice-of-law amendment or evaluate alternative cyber carriers with AZ choice-of-law.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa §8.36 Confidentiality / Data Protection Controls — Cyber Alignment
findings.contract_quote: The Contractor shall establish and maintain procedures and controls that are adequate to assure that no information contained in its records and/or obtained from the County or from others in carrying out its functions (services) under the contract shall be used by or disclosed by it, its agents, officers, or employees, except as required to efficiently perform duties under the contract... If, at any time during the duration of the contract, the County determines that the procedures and controls in place are not adequate, the Contractor shall institute any new and/or additional measures requested by the County within 15 business days of the written request to do so.
findings.policy_quote: AmTrust Cyber Privacy and Network Security Coverage Limit $4,000,000 (shared, eroding).
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.36 requires Run-Test to maintain data security controls and to implement County-required additional measures within 15 business days of written request. The Cyber policy is the financial backstop for any breach of these obligations. Cyber adequacy issues in Findings 002-006 (limit deficiency, retro gap, AI/WoS missing, social engineering phantom) all bear directly on §8.36 alignment. Operationally, Run-Test should maintain documented data security control framework (NIST CSF, ISO 27001, or SOC 2) to demonstrate compliance and respond quickly to County requests.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires you to maintain data security controls AND respond to any County request to upgrade controls within 15 business days. Your cyber policy is the financial backstop for any breach of those duties — and the cyber policy has multiple structural problems already flagged. Operationally, you need documented controls (SOC 2 or ISO 27001 certification helps) to respond quickly to County demands. Don't wait for the request — pre-build the framework.
findings.recommendation: (1) Document current data security control framework (recommend SOC 2 Type II for vendor-of-record positioning); (2) Pre-build incident response runbook aligned with Maricopa breach notification expectations; (3) Resolve Cyber findings (002-006) to ensure financial backstop matches operational obligations; (4) Establish 15-business-day rapid-response protocol for County control upgrade requests.
discoveryQuestions: Do you currently hold SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certification? Counties increasingly require it — and it's the cleanest evidence of §8.36 control adequacy.
If Maricopa sent a written request tomorrow demanding new data security controls within 15 business days, what's your operational capability to respond? Does IT have surge capacity?
Has anyone benchmarked your current controls against NIST CSF or CIS Controls? A formal gap assessment is usually a good investment given your voter PII exposure profile.

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa Notification of Claim (30/10 Days) and Sacramento (30/10 Days)
findings.contract_quote: (Sacramento §X) CONTRACTOR shall give prompt and timely notice thereof to COUNTY. Notice shall be prompt and timely if given within thirty (30) days following the date of receipt of a claim or ten (10) days following the date of service of process of a lawsuit. (Maricopa §8.2.15 contractor 2-business-day carrier-receipt notification.)
findings.contract_page: Sacramento §X, Page 4 of 4; Maricopa §8.2.15, Page 7 of 41
findings.policy_quote: N/A — operational obligation independent of policy mechanics.
findings.gap_description: Both contracts impose direct contractual notice obligations that are SEPARATE from carrier notice triggers. Sacramento: 30 days post-claim-receipt, 10 days post-service-of-process to County. Maricopa: 2 business days from carrier policy notice receipt. Trigger language is broad ('directly or indirectly, contingently or otherwise, affect or might reasonably affect COUNTY'). Run-Test must build internal claims-management protocol that bifurcates carrier notice from County notice. Failure is contract breach, not coverage denial — but contract breach can trigger termination rights.
findings.plain_english: Both counties want direct notice of claims and lawsuits — separately from your carrier notice. Sacramento: 30 days for a claim, 10 days for a lawsuit. Maricopa: 2 business days from when your carrier notifies you of any policy issue. This is an operational compliance requirement, not an insurance issue. Build it into your legal/risk-management workflow.
findings.recommendation: Build internal claims protocol: (1) Any claim or lawsuit involving Run-Test triggers parallel notice to applicable counties; (2) Maintain county notice contact list with current addresses; (3) Document delivery confirmation; (4) Train executive team and legal/risk personnel on dual notice obligations.
discoveryQuestions: When you get sued or receive a claim that 'might reasonably affect' a county, you have 30 days (Sacramento) or 2 business days (Maricopa-related) to notify the county directly. Is that built into your legal team's workflow? Most companies don't build the parallel notice obligation in.
Have you ever missed a contractual notice deadline on a county claim? Even if the substantive claim was handled, missing the notice deadline can trigger county termination rights.

findings.requirement_type: Subcontractor Insurance Compliance Program
findings.contract_quote: (Sacramento §VII.E) CONTRACTOR shall be responsible for the acts and omissions of all its subcontractors and additional insured endorsements as provided by CONTRACTORs subcontractor.
findings.policy_quote: 00 GL1053 00 01 25 (Independent Contractor Requirements Endorsement on Arch Security Guards): 'Insured must obtain COIs from independent contractors with limits ≥ insured's CGL limits. Failure does not eliminate coverage but converts contractor's costs to premium basis at contractor classifications.' Hanover GL has standard CG 00 01 subcontractor work giveback for products-completed operations hazard.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §VII.E requires Run-Test to be responsible for sub acts/omissions and to obtain AI endorsements from subs. Run-Test likely uses subcontractors for: (a) printing — high-volume ballot printing may be subcontracted to specialty printers; (b) mailing — bulk mail handling is often subcontracted to mail-house operators; (c) IT/software — tech services. Without a documented sub-insurance compliance program (COI collection, AI endorsement verification, minimum-limit enforcement, subcontract flow-down clauses), Run-Test is exposed both contractually (Sacramento breach) and financially (uninsured sub claims).
findings.plain_english: Sacramento makes you responsible for any of your subcontractors' mistakes, and requires you to collect AI endorsements from your subs that name the County. If you don't have a documented program for verifying that your printers, mail houses, IT consultants, and other subs carry adequate insurance and have endorsed the County as AI, you're exposed both ways: you eat their claims if uninsured, and Sacramento can call it a contract breach.
findings.recommendation: (1) Build subcontractor insurance compliance program: minimum required limits, mandatory AI/WoS endorsements, sub-insurance verification at contract signing, annual COI re-collection. (2) Standardize subcontract template with insurance flow-down clauses mirroring county-level requirements (Sacramento §VII, Maricopa §8.2). (3) Use COI tracking software (myCOI, EBIX, Trust Layer) to systematize verification. (4) Audit current sub portfolio for compliance gaps.
discoveryQuestions: Do you have a documented program for collecting and verifying COIs from your subcontractors — printers, mail houses, IT consultants? What's the average time-to-verification?
If a sub causes a loss that's pinned on Run-Test, do you have COIs and AI endorsements that flow the loss back to their carrier? Without that, you absorb the loss directly.
Sacramento expressly requires you to collect AI endorsements from your subs naming the County. Has anyone audited the current sub portfolio against that standard?

findings.requirement_type: AmTrust Cyber — No Standalone Designated Entity NOC
findings.contract_quote: (Maricopa §8.2.15) Contractor's insurance shall not be permitted to expire, be suspended, be canceled, or be materially changed for any reason without 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County.
findings.policy_quote: Item 8 Endorsements list shows blank in extracted text; no designated entity NOC endorsement located on AmTrust Cyber.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa §8.2.15 expressly applies to ALL insurance policies required under the contract — Cyber is required under §8.2.13. The AmTrust Cyber policy has no visible Designated Entity NOC endorsement scheduling Maricopa County. Combined with Findings 006 (no AI/WoS/P&NC) and 002-005 (limit/scope deficiencies), Cyber is the most contractually-deficient policy in the program against Maricopa requirements.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa requires 30-day cancellation notice on EVERY required policy — including cyber. Your cyber policy doesn't have Maricopa on a notice-of-cancellation endorsement at all. So if AmTrust cancels mid-term, Maricopa never gets notice — and that's a contract breach independent of all the other cyber problems.
findings.recommendation: Request AmTrust issue Designated Entity NOC endorsement scheduling Maricopa, Sacramento, and Los Angeles Counties at 30-day notice (or longer per broker target of 90 days). If AmTrust will not endorse, this is another reason to market the cyber placement at renewal.
discoveryQuestions: Your cyber policy has no notice-of-cancellation endorsement scheduling any of your county clients. If AmTrust cancels mid-term, the counties never get carrier-direct notice. Is that consistent with your contract obligations? It isn't.
When you bound the AmTrust cyber, was the broker asked to schedule Maricopa, Sacramento, and Los Angeles on the NOC? It's the kind of detail that gets lost in renewal cycles.

findings.requirement_type: Hartford Crime — Acts by LLC Members Carve-Out
findings.contract_quote: N/A — internal coverage limitation given LLC entity structure.
findings.policy_quote: PP 00 H600 00 0616 §V(B): 'Excludes loss from theft/deception fraud/forgery committed by partners or LLC members. As an LLC, Runbeck's LLC-member-perpetrated crime is excluded except limited carve-back for IA 1 (Employee Theft) and IA 2 (Forgery) subject to LLC-member-as-Employee paragraph (10) calculation.'
findings.gap_description: Crime policy excludes losses from theft/deception/forgery committed by partners or LLC members of the Insured Entity. Run-Test is an LLC. Limited carve-back exists for Employee Theft (IA 1) and Forgery (IA 2) subject to LLC-member-as-Employee calculation. PE-backed structures often have LLC manager/member roles where individuals could be characterized as 'members' rather than 'employees' — material gap for executive-level theft scenarios. Worth confirming whether Run-Test's day-to-day operating leadership are technically LLC members or employees.
findings.plain_english: Your Crime policy carves out theft by LLC members. Since you're an LLC, this matters: if a managing member or principal commits the theft, the standard exclusion can bar recovery. Limited carve-back for Employee Theft and Forgery, but the calculation is fact-specific. Worth confirming with the carrier exactly how they'd treat your operating leadership in a theft scenario.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm with Hartford in writing how the LLC-member-as-Employee carve-back paragraph (10) applies to Runbeck's actual organizational structure. (2) Identify operating-leadership individuals whose theft would be most material (CFO, controller, CEO, treasurer) and verify their characterization as members vs. employees. (3) If gap material, evaluate alternative Crime markets that don't have this LLC carve-out.
discoveryQuestions: Are your operating executives (CEO, CFO, controller) technically LLC members or employees? If members, your Crime policy may not respond to executive-level theft. Has anyone confirmed how Hartford would treat their roles?

What's your control environment around principal-level financial authority? Banking signatures, wire transfer authorities, vendor approvals — who has them, and would they fit the 'LLC member' definition that's excluded from Crime?

findings.requirement_type: E&O Hammer Clause 80/20 — Settlement Pressure
findings.contract_quote: N/A — settlement-mechanic feature.
findings.policy_quote: Endorsement #16 (VP 08 51 05 17 — Consent to Settle Amendment Hammer Clause): '80/20 hammer clause — if Named Insured refuses Company's recommended settlement, carrier liability capped at recommended settlement amount + 80% of Claim Expenses and Loss in excess of recommended amount. Insured bears 20%.'
findings.gap_description: Standard 80/20 hammer clause on Gemini E&O. If Run-Test refuses a carrier-recommended settlement, Run-Test bears 20% of subsequent defense costs and any judgment in excess of the recommended amount. Standard market language but creates real economic pressure to accept settlements that may damage reputation/competitive position. Election services involves repeat county clients; settlement of disputed claims may be more strategically costly than the dollars suggest.
findings.plain_english: If Gemini wants you to settle a claim and you refuse, you eat 20% of all future defense costs and any extra judgment dollars. Standard market language, but for an election services vendor where settling can signal weakness to county clients, that 20% pressure is real. Worth understanding the mechanic before a claim hits.
findings.recommendation: (1) Educate executive team on hammer clause economics; (2) At renewal, attempt to negotiate to 90/10 or 95/5 hammer (sometimes available); (3) Consider standalone Reputation Defense coverage for high-stakes settlements where reputational stakes outweigh monetary economics.
discoveryQuestions: If Gemini recommends settling a county lawsuit for $750K and you'd rather fight, you bear 20% of future defense costs and any extra judgment. For an election technology vendor where settling can signal weakness to county clients, what's your appetite for that pressure?
Has the carrier's claims team been responsive enough that you trust their settlement recommendations? Or is there friction that would lead you to override?

findings.requirement_type: Hanover Property — Sprinkler Protective Safeguards Warranty
findings.contract_quote: N/A — operational compliance warranty.
findings.policy_quote: CP 04 11 09 17 (Protective Safeguards): 'Schedule lists Premises 1, Building 1, Symbol P-1 (Automatic Sprinkler System). Insured must maintain sprinkler system in working order and notify carrier of any suspension/impairment (>48 hours). Failure to comply triggers fire exclusion.'
findings.gap_description: Property policy contains Protective Safeguards warranty requiring sprinkler system maintenance and 48-hour impairment notice. Failure to comply triggers full fire exclusion. For a printing/manufacturing operation with $21M+ blanket building and $16M+ blanket personal property values plus $11.5M business income exposure, sprinkler impairment without notice could result in catastrophic uninsured fire loss. Warranty management is operational discipline issue.
findings.plain_english: Your property policy has a clause that says: if your sprinkler is offline for more than 48 hours and you don't tell the carrier, fire claims are denied. With $50M+ in property and business income exposure, this is a high-stakes warranty. Make sure your facilities team knows the 48-hour notification rule and has a tested escalation path.
findings.recommendation: (1) Document sprinkler impairment notification procedure; (2) Train facilities and security on 48-hour rule; (3) Maintain inspection/maintenance log per NFPA 25; (4) Pre-establish broker contact for impairment notification.
discoveryQuestions: Does your facilities team know that a sprinkler impairment over 48 hours, without carrier notice, voids fire coverage? With $50M+ in exposed values, that's a big-stakes warranty.
When was the last full sprinkler inspection per NFPA 25? Annual? Quarterly? Documented?
Who in operations has the authority and process to notify Hanover within 48 hours of a sprinkler impairment? Is the broker contact information posted in the security office?

findings.requirement_type: Hanover GL Conflicting Pollution Exclusions (CG 21 49 vs CG 21 55)
findings.contract_quote: N/A — internal policy form conflict.
findings.policy_quote: CG 21 49 09 99 (Total Pollution Exclusion Endorsement): absolute exclusion, no hostile fire exception. CG 21 55 09 99 (Total Pollution Exclusion With A Hostile Fire Exception): includes hostile fire exception. Both forms are attached.
findings.gap_description: Two conflicting pollution exclusions are attached to the Hanover GL. CG 21 49 is absolute (no hostile fire carve-back); CG 21 55 includes the hostile fire exception. In a coverage dispute, the more restrictive form (CG 21 49) typically controls. Carrier intent should be confirmed in writing — likely a renewal-cycle clerical error rather than deliberate underwriting choice. Either exclusion is broader than necessary; CG 21 65 (with hostile fire AND additional limited carve-backs) may be more appropriate for a printing/manufacturing operation.
findings.plain_english: Your GL has two pollution exclusions attached that say different things — one absolute, one with a hostile fire exception. In a coverage dispute the broader exclusion wins, which means the absolute one. Probably just a clerical error from prior renewal cycles. Get a written confirmation from Hanover and remove the duplicate at renewal.
findings.recommendation: Request Hanover endorsement clarifying which pollution exclusion controls. Recommend removing CG 21 49 (absolute) and retaining CG 21 55 (with hostile fire exception). Combine with Finding 013 recommendation to add CPL.

findings.requirement_type: Sacramento §IX Course of Construction (COC) WoS — Inapplicable
findings.contract_quote: Course of Construction (COC) Waiver of Subrogation: Any Course of Construction (COC) policies maintained by the CONTRACTOR in performance of the Agreement shall contain the following provisions: 1. The COUNTY shall be named as loss payee. 2. The Insurer shall waive all rights of subrogation against the COUNTY.
findings.policy_quote: N/A — no Builder's Risk / COC policy in program.
findings.gap_description: Sacramento §IX contemplates Builder's Risk / Course of Construction policies. Inapplicable to Run-Test as election services do not involve construction. If any future county engagement involves a project component characterized as construction (facility build-out, installation construction, etc.), the COC requirement triggers. Currently no exposure; properly omitted.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento has a Builder's Risk requirement that doesn't apply to election services. Properly omitted. Watch for any future county engagement that includes construction components — the requirement would re-trigger.
findings.recommendation: No current action required. Flag for review if any future county contract includes construction or facility build-out components.

findings.requirement_type: Hanover GL — Cyber Incident Endorsement (421-5286) Restricts Beyond Standard CG Forms
findings.contract_quote: (Sacramento §II.A) The General Liability shall be on an Occurrence basis... [implicit ISO CG 0001 'without additional exclusions or limitations, unless approved by the County Risk Manager' standard].
findings.policy_quote: 421-5286 01 25 (Exclusion — Cyber Incident — Cyber Content): 'Absolute exclusion for BI/PD/PI&AI caused by, arising out of or as a consequence of a cyber incident. Defines cyber incident broadly: unauthorized access, malicious code, denial of service, plus IP/copyright/trademark infringement, plagiarism, invasion of right of publicity, and defamation arising from electronic cyber content.'
findings.gap_description: Hanover-proprietary 421-5286 endorsement is broader than ISO CG 40 35 (Cyber Incident Exclusion). It also pulls in cyber-content offenses (IP infringement, plagiarism, right of publicity, defamation) when delivered electronically — meaning traditional Personal & Advertising Injury offenses are stripped out when the offense occurs through electronic media. For an election services vendor with website, voter portal, online ballot tracking, social media presence, and electronic communications, this materially narrows Coverage B (Personal & Advertising Injury). Sacramento §II.A 'no additional exclusions' standard implicates this endorsement.
findings.plain_english: Hanover added their own cyber endorsement that goes beyond standard ISO language. It strips out Personal & Advertising Injury coverage whenever the offense happens through electronic media — so any IP infringement, defamation, or right-of-publicity claim arising from your website or voter portal isn't covered. Combined with the standard cyber and data privacy exclusions, your Coverage B is very limited for online activity. Worth requesting Sacramento Risk Manager approval or marketing to a carrier with cleaner forms.
findings.recommendation: Request Sacramento Risk Manager waiver of the 421-5286 endorsement. At renewal, evaluate alternative GL markets without this proprietary endorsement (Travelers, Chubb, AIG often write cleaner Coverage B for election technology vendors).
findings.covered_by_which_policy: AmTrust Cyber Media coverage ($4M shared) responds to some scenarios but with limit/structural deficiencies (Findings 002-006).
discoveryQuestions: If a candidate sues Run-Test for defamation arising from how their name appeared on a digital ballot tracker on your website, your GL Personal & Advertising Injury coverage is excluded. Did anyone walk you through this Hanover-proprietary endorsement at bind?

Election technology vendors increasingly face online defamation, right-of-publicity, and IP infringement claims tied to digital ballot tracking and voter information portals. Has your cyber policy been sized to absorb the full Coverage B gap on the GL?

For data privacy obligations, longer retention is sometimes advisable. For litigation-defense record availability, longer is better. Operational compliance issue, not a coverage gap.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants you to keep records for 6 years after final payment. That aligns roughly with your claims-made tail and is a manageable operational standard. Make sure your records management policy reflects the requirement.

findings.requirement_type: Disaster Recovery / Business Continuity — Maricopa Exhibit C Alignment
findings.contract_quote: Contractor shall provide a contingency (Disaster Recovery) plan to MCED, coordinate said plan with the MCED, and provide expeditious emergency services to be exercised in the event of natural disaster, or other emergency, the causes of which are beyond the control of the Contractor and the MCED.
findings.contract_page: Maricopa Exhibit B §2.1.15, Page 25 of 41; Exhibit C, Pages 38-40 of 41
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Property Business Income $11.5M, 80% coinsurance, 60-day extended period of indemnity, 72-hour time deductible. Equipment Breakdown Business Income $11.5M. AmTrust Cyber Business Interruption $4M (shared aggregate, 8-hour waiting period, 180-day Period of Restoration). Cyber BI from Suppliers $4M (shared, 8-hour waiting, 180-day PoR).
findings.policy_page: Hanover Property Page 154; AmTrust Cyber Page 3
findings.gap_description: Maricopa Exhibit C details disaster recovery requirements: data backup, alternate-site production, materials warehousing, expeditious emergency services. Property BI ($11.5M) covers physical-cause BI. Cyber BI ($4M shared aggregate) covers cyber-cause BI. Two structural gaps: (1) Cyber BI shares the $4M aggregate with all other cyber coverages — a real cyber event consuming $2M elsewhere leaves $2M for BI; (2) 60-day Extended Period of Indemnity on property BI may be inadequate for election cycle — election work has compressed timeline windows where a 60-day BI extension may not align with revenue restoration. Election-cycle BI exposure is highly seasonal and event-driven; standard 60-day extended periods may understate reality.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa has detailed disaster recovery requirements — backup data, alternate sites, emergency services. Your Property BI is $11.5M (good limit) but Cyber BI is part of the shared $4M cyber aggregate (after a ransomware event, BI capacity may be near-zero). Your election-cycle revenue is seasonal — a property loss before a major election could cost more than $11.5M of BI provides. Worth re-evaluating BI limits with election-cycle revenue patterns in mind.
findings.recommendation: (1) Model election-cycle revenue exposure: peak revenue months × business-recovery time. Verify $11.5M is adequate. (2) Increase Cyber BI sublimit to non-shared structure if available. (3) Consider Contingent Business Interruption coverage for Cyber BI from key suppliers (printers, mail houses, IT vendors). (4) Document DRP per Maricopa Exhibit C and align cyber/property insurance scope with operational recovery plan.
discoveryQuestions: What's your peak-month revenue during a federal election cycle vs. a quiet month? If a property fire or cyber event hits in October of a federal election year, is $11.5M of BI enough to bridge the recovery? Most election-services vendors I've audited need more.
Maricopa's Exhibit C details a Disaster Recovery Plan. Has yours been formally documented and shared with Maricopa? §2.1.15 requires coordination with MCED.

Your Cyber BI shares the $4M aggregate with everything else. After a $2M ransomware response, you have $2M of BI left. Has the cyber renewal team modeled non-shared BI sublimits at the next placement?

findings.requirement_type: Cancellation Notice Cadence — Mixed Across Program (Broker Target 90 Days)
findings.contract_quote: (Maricopa §8.2.15) 30 days prior written notice to Maricopa County. (Sacramento §VI.A.2) Insured-burdened 'immediately notify County.'
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Auto: 60 days other reasons (461-0155 #1). Hanover GL/Property: 45 days (AZ amendatory IL 02 58). Hanover WC: 30 days (AZ WC 02 06 01 C). Hanover Umbrella: 45 days (475-0176 AZ Changes). Hartford Mgmt Liab: AZ — only nonpayment cancellation (10 days), no other cancellation (Endt #32 / HR 02 H003 01). Gemini E&O: 60 days. Convex Excess: not specified. AmTrust Cyber: not specified. Designated Entity NOC: 30 days where applicable.
findings.gap_description: Cancellation notice periods range from 10 days (Hartford AZ amendatory) to 60 days (Auto/E&O), with most at 30-45 days. Broker target per RMF General All Policies #1 is 90 days. Maricopa requires 30 days and is met by all. Sacramento places notice burden on Insured. The most restrictive period in the program is the Hartford AZ amendatory (10 days nonpayment) — but Hartford notably will NOT cancel for any reason other than nonpayment in AZ, which is favorable. Designated entity NOC missing for Maricopa, Sacramento, LA (Finding 008). No 90-day notice anywhere in program.
findings.plain_english: Cancellation notices range from 10 days to 60 days across your policies — the broker industry target is 90 days, and you're not there anywhere. Maricopa's 30-day requirement is met everywhere, but if they wanted longer, you don't have it. At renewal, push every carrier for 90-day notice (most will give it on a designated entity NOC endorsement at minimal cost).
findings.recommendation: At each renewal, request 90-day cancellation/non-renewal notice on Designated Entity NOC endorsements. Standardize across program where carriers permit. Document any non-conforming carriers.
discoveryQuestions: Industry best-practice for commercial brokers is 90 days of cancellation notice on every required policy. You're at 30-45 days mostly. At your premium volume, every carrier should be willing to extend to 90 — has the broker requested it?
If a county invokes its insurance-spec termination rights and you have only 30 days to replace coverage, can you actually do it? Cyber and Tech E&O can take longer than that to remarket and bind.

findings.requirement_type: Hanover Property — Special Theft Sublimits (Patterns/Dies/Molds $5K)
findings.contract_quote: N/A — sublimit adequacy issue for printing operations.
findings.policy_quote: 411-0793 02 23 Special Theft Sublimits: furs $10K, jewelry $10K, precious metals $35K, patterns/dies/molds $5K, tickets $1K.
findings.gap_description: Patterns/Dies/Molds theft sublimit at $5,000 is materially low for a printing operation. Election ballot printing involves specialized printing plates, dies, embossing tools, and security-feature dies that can each individually exceed $5K in replacement cost. Theft of an entire printing setup would expose the operation to direct uninsured loss. Tickets sublimit ($1K) likely irrelevant.
findings.plain_english: Theft of patterns, dies, or molds — used in your printing operations — is capped at $5,000. Printing dies for a single ballot run can cost $50K+ each. If a competitor or insider stole your election printing setup, you'd be paying out of pocket to replace. Worth bumping the sublimit up.
findings.recommendation: At Property renewal: increase Patterns/Dies/Molds theft sublimit to $50K-$100K based on inventory replacement cost. Document inventory of dies/plates/setups for underwriter review.
discoveryQuestions: What's the replacement cost of a complete ballot printing setup — plates, dies, embossing tools, security-feature dies? Your policy caps theft at $5K. Single-die replacement often exceeds that.
Have you ever had die/plate theft or insider misappropriation of printing setups? Election technology IP is increasingly attractive to competitors.
